paragraphs.heading: What the idea says
paragraphs.text: The Late Heavy Bombardment, also called the lunar cataclysm, is a proposed event in the early Solar System. The idea is that roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, an unusually large number of asteroids and comets struck the worlds of the inner Solar System: Mercury, Venus, Earth and its Moon, and Mars. It remains a hypothesis. Scientists once widely accepted it, and now they debate it.

paragraphs.heading: The clue in the Apollo rocks
paragraphs.text: The evidence comes from Moon rocks that Apollo astronauts carried home. The key samples are impact melts, rocks that were last molten during an impact. Most of them are thought to have formed when asteroids or comets tens of kilometres across hit the Moon and dug craters hundreds of kilometres wide. When the melts were dated, their ages seemed to bunch between about 3.8 and 4.1 billion years. Investigators read that bunching as the record of an intense battering of the Moon, and proposed that the rate of impacts rose dramatically around 3.9 billion years ago.

paragraphs.heading: A possible cause
paragraphs.text: Several explanations have been offered for this apparent spike in impacts, and none has won general agreement. One that is popular among planetary scientists is called the Nice model. It proposes that the giant planets shifted their orbits. As they moved, they scattered objects from the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt, or both, into the path of the inner planets.

paragraphs.heading: A second look from meteorites
paragraphs.text: More data have since come from lunar meteorites. They are thought to sample the lunar surface at random, and at least some should come from places far from where Apollo landed. Some probably came from the far side of the Moon, and impact melts inside these have been dated. None turned out older than about 3.9 billion years. That fits the cataclysm idea. Yet the ages do not bunch at that date; they are spread between 2.5 and 3.9 billion years.

paragraphs.heading: One impact or many
paragraphs.text: Critics raise two main objections. The first is about where the Apollo melts came from. They have usually been credited to whichever basin lay closest to each landing site, but a large share may instead come from one basin, Imbrium. Among the multi-ring basins on the central near side of the Moon, Imbrium is both the youngest and the largest, and modelling shows that a significant amount of its debris should lie at every Apollo landing site. If so, the cluster of ages near 3.9 billion years records a single impact and not several.

paragraphs.heading: The missing older rocks
paragraphs.text: The second objection concerns the absence of impact melts older than about 4.1 billion years. Older melts may once have existed and had their ages reset by the steady cratering of the past 4 billion years. They may also have been crushed into pieces too small to date by standard methods. A range of evidence points instead to a longer stretch of bombardment of the Moon, from about 4.2 to 3.5 billion years ago. Firm evidence either way is still lacking.

paragraphs.heading: What it meant for early Earth
paragraphs.text: Before this hypothesis was framed, geologists generally assumed that Earth stayed molten until about 3.8 billion years ago. That date turned up in many of the oldest known rocks around the world, and no older rocks could be found. It was used to mark the boundary between the earlier Hadean eon and the later Archean eon. Then, in 1999, a rock from the Acasta Gneiss in northwestern Canada was dated to 4.031 billion years old, the oldest known rock on Earth.
